newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia ready to withdraw last troops from Chechnya.
newsitem.headline: Russia ready to withdraw last troops from Chechnya.

text.p: Russia prepared to start pulling out its remaining troops from Chechnya on Wednesday in line with pledges made by President Boris Yeltsin and ahead of elections in the breakaway region set for January.

But the Foreign Ministry, anxious to quash the separatists' ambitions, warned other countries against moving to establish diplomatic ties with Chechnya, whose final political status has been deferred for five years under an August peace deal.

Interfax news agency, quoting a ministry source, said any country allowing the Chechen rebels to set up an embassy on its territory would be taking "an unfriendly step that cast doubt on Russia's territorial integrity."
"Such steps would trigger the most serious consequences and might lead to a rupture in diplomatic relations (with Moscow)," Interfax quoted the source as saying.

Russia was stung by a recent interview given by Chechen government leader Aslan Maskhadov to a Saudi newspaper in which he reportedly said the rebels' representative offices abroad could become embassies.
In the interview Maskhadov also reportedly thanked fighters from Arab and other Islamic countries for helping the Chechen rebels during their 21-month battle against Russian troops.
"In such a case we would be speaking of direct foreign intervention in Russia's internal affairs," the Foreign Ministry source said.
The Defence Ministry plans to start pulling out its last troops from Chechnya on December 1 and the withdrawal will be completed by January 25, Interfax said.
Interior Ministry spokesman Vasily Panchenkov told Reuters his ministry would also withdraw its troops but gave no deadline, saying more would be known after November 30.

Russia has already withdrawn the bulk of its troops from Chechnya following the August 31 peace treaty but had wanted to leave two units permanently in Chechnya -- one from the Defence Ministry and another from the Interior Ministry.

Last Saturday, in a surprise order that infuriated his communist and nationalist opponents in the State Duma lower house of parliament, Yeltsin agreed to withdraw these two units, thereby meeting all rebel demands except full independence.

Moscow, forced to acknowledge defeat in its bloody military campaign to keep Chechnya inside the Russian Federation, is now trying to retain control with economic inducements and has proposed setting up a free trade zone in the region.
Yeltsin's foes plan to hold an extraordinary parliamentary session on Friday to discuss the issue of troop withdrawal, which they argue effectively sanctions Chechen independence.
They have threatened to try to impeach Yeltsin -- a long drawn-out procedure which has little chance of success -- or to call for a no-confidence vote in the government.
Ultra-nationalist Vladimir Zhirinovsky said concessions to the Chechen rebels would spark similiar demands in other Russian regions, leading to the country's break-up.
"The government is pursuing an anti-Russian course...Russia will end up with just 100th of its present territory," he told a news conference.

The secretary of Russia's Security Council, Ivan Rybkin, discussed the situation in Chechnya on Wednesday with Yeltsin's chief-of-staff Anatoly Chubais and Interior Minister Anatoly Kulikov in separate meetings.

In Chechnya itself, the commander of Russian federal forces, Vladimir Sukhoruchenko, and the Chechen chief of staff reached agreement "on all questions" relating to the practical withdrawal of Moscow's troops, RIA news agency said.
It quoted Sukhoruchenko as saying the Chechens had agreed to provide an escort to guarantee the security of his troops.
Elections to set up a post-war administration in Chechnya are scheduled for January 27 and the polling campaign officially began on Wednesday.
Chechen separatist leader Zelimkhan Yandarbiyev has already said he plans to run for the presidency.

Another possible candidate is the respected Aslan Maskhadov, who commanded the guerrillas who beat off the Russian army, though he has so far shown loyalty to Yandarbiyev in order to avoid a split in separatist ranks.
Tass said Doku Zavgayev, the Kremlin-backed official who ran Chechnya during the war and who now lives in Moscow, would not return to the region to run in the election.
